name: Wealthfront
foundedNote: Two separate S-1 exhibits certify the same charter date: Exhibit 3.1 (Restated Certificate, dated 2022-09-22) and Exhibit 3.2 (post-IPO Amended and Restated Certificate) both open 'The date of the filing of its original Certificate of Incorporation with the Secretary of State of the State of Delaware was January 5, 2007 ... originally incorporated under the name of MAJ I, Inc.' The S-1 body agrees: 'We were incorporated in the State of Delaware in January 2007 as MAJ I, Inc. We changed our name to Kaching Group Inc. in January 2008 and then to Wealthfront Inc. in October 2010. In August 2018, we changed our name to Wealthfront Corporation.' Two dates in circulation are wrong for this purpose. EDGAR's former-name metadata records the Wealthfront Inc. rename as 2011-06-30, which is the date the name first reached the filing system, not the charter date (the S-1 says October 2010). And every secondary source dates the company to the team founding: Forbes says 'Cofounded in 2008 by Andy Rachleff', VatorNews says January 2008 with Daniel Carroll, and both are describing kaChing, the mutual-fund marketplace that preceded the robo-advisor. Because MAJ I, Inc. is the same continuously existing Delaware corporation that trades today as WLTH — never dissolved, never reincorporated — the earliest-formal-founding rule puts t=0 at 2007-01-05, roughly a year before the founding date every profile of the company prints.

annualOverrides.note: IPO day. 34,615,384 shares priced at $14.00 on 2025-12-11 (21,468,038 primary, 13,147,346 secondary); the 424B4 cover states 146,268,749 shares outstanding after the offering, so 146,268,749 x $14.00 = $2,047,762,486. Trading opened at $14.00 on 2025-12-12 and closed at $14.19, which would put the closing figure at $2.08B; the offering price is used because both of its inputs come from the prospectus. The '$2.7 billion' printed by some debut coverage is a fully diluted number and is not comparable to the series.

events.note: Exists only in the S-1 preferred-stock note: 1,350,000 shares at an $0.11 issuance price, liquidation preference $149K. Below the inclusion floor and never plotted. The S-1 gives no issue date; 2008 is an inference from the January 2008 rename to Kaching Group Inc. and the December 2008 angel round, and the shares could have been issued as early as 2007. Recorded at year precision for that reason.

events.nameConflict: Charter Series B, but no outlet ever called it that; contemporaneous coverage says only 'an angel round'.
events.note: 7,658,868 shares at $0.39 (S-1 cap table) = $2,986,959, matching the '$3 million previously raised' TechCrunch cited a year later. Below the inclusion floor on the mechanical test: TechCrunch's December 2008 piece names Marc Andreessen, Ben Horowitz, Kevin Compton, Doug Mackenzie, Bruce Dunlevie, Jeff Jordan and Andy Rachleff and says explicitly that all of them 'invested personally rather than through their firms'. No named firm led it, so it is recorded and not plotted.

events.nameConflict: Some outlets called it a Series A because it was the first round with a firm lead; the charter letter is C.
events.note: This is the inclusion floor — the first round led by a named venture firm. 5,952,858 shares at $1.27 = $7,560,130; press rounded to $7.5M. Dated to the TechCrunch announcement; the closing date is not disclosed anywhere. No valuation was published, so it carries an amount and no vertex.

events.nameConflict: TechCrunch called this a Series B and reported total funding of $30.5M against the charter's fourth series. Press numbering runs two letters behind the charter throughout Wealthfront's history because Series A-C were issued under the kaChing name.
events.note: 14,431,844 shares at $1.36 = $19,627,308. Greylock Partners and The Social+Capital Partnership participated. No valuation disclosed. TechCrunch's '$30.5 million raised to date' is a good independent check on the cap table: A+B+C+D derives to $30.32M.

The Form D filed 2014-04-04 gives a first sale date of 2014-04-02 and a total sold of exactly $34,999,969 — the company aimed at $35.0M and landed $31 short of it. The cap table's 8,780,133 shares at a rounded $3.99 implies $35.03M; the Form D figure is used because it is the actual cash. No valuation disclosed.

events.roundName: $64M round led by Spark Capital Growth
events.nameConflict: Widely labelled Series D by press and databases; the charter letter is F.
events.note: The Form D and the S-1 cap table agree to the dollar: first sale 2014-10-28, $64,172,931 sold, and 7,816,435 shares at $8.21 = $64,172,931.35. The $700M valuation is not from a filing — it comes from press coverage (Finovate, Vox, Reuters) and Wealthfront never confirmed it, so it is marked soft. It is one of only two rounds in nine with any public valuation at all, which is the normal state of affairs rather than a gap.

events.nameConflict: Usually labelled Series E in databases; the charter letter is G.
events.note: A down round: $700M at Series F to about $500M here. The primary record corroborates the direction independently of the press — the S-1 cap table prices Series G at $3.97 per share against Series F's $8.21, a 52% cut in the per-share price on the same split basis. The $500M figure itself is a single Bloomberg story of 2018-03-23 (read via InvestmentNews' syndication), and a Wealthfront spokesperson 'disputed the latest valuation but declined to give the current number', so it is soft rather than confirmed. The company's January 2018 press release announcing the round states no valuation. Dated to the closing rather than the 2018-01-04 announcement: the amended and restated Investors' Rights Agreement entered at the Series G/G-1 closing is dated 2017-12-27 (S-1 Exhibit 4.2 recital), and Bloomberg said the round 'closed in late 2017'. 18,889,279 shares at $3.97 = $74,990,438.

A $25M financing with no press coverage anywhere — it surfaces only in the S-1 preferred-stock note, which is exactly the case for reading the cap table rather than the coverage. 5,034,942 shares at $4.97 = $25,023,662, a 25% premium to the Series G price struck at essentially the same time. Neither the lead nor the participants can be identified: Exhibit 4.2's investor schedule is a single combined list for all series, so `institutional` is left null rather than asserting either answer. The only date anchor is that the G-1 holders are already recited as Prior Investors in the 2017-12-27 Investors' Rights Agreement, so it closed on or before that date.

UBS announced on 2022-01-26 that it 'would acquire Wealthfront in an all-cash transaction valued at $1.4 billion'. The two parties mutually terminated the merger agreement on 2022-09-02. Never plotted: no one ever transacted at this price, so putting it on the line would assert a mark that never existed. The price is kept because UBS re-struck it as a note the same day it walked away — see the next event.

Money genuinely changed hands here, unlike the terminated acquisition, so this is the plotted event. The S-1 financing note: 'On September 2, 2022, the Company issued a $69.7 million convertible note with a maturity date of September 2, 2025 ... at a conversion price of $9.54 per share', and the cap table reserves 7,305,567 Series H-1 and 7,305,567 Series H-2 shares at a $9.54 issuance price, none ever issued. The counterparty is never named in the S-1 body — `grep -c UBS` on it returns 0 — and appears only in Exhibit 4.2, which recites the Convertible Note Purchase Agreement with UBS Americas Inc. dated 2022-09-02. The $1.4B is an ESTIMATE, not a reported figure: $9.54 across a then fully diluted base of roughly 147M shares reproduces the $1.4B UBS had agreed to pay in January, i.e. UBS re-priced the dead deal as a note. No party ever published a valuation for the note. It was repaid in full in March 2024 and never converted.

Initiated August 2024 for up to 2,468,413 shares held by then-current employees; in September 2024 the company repurchased 1,996,765 shares at $11.76 for $23.5M. No amount is recorded as raised because the cash flowed out, not in. Forbes wrote at the S-1 that Wealthfront 'was last valued at $2 billion in a 2024 tender offer, when it let employees sell their private Wealthfront stock' — a rounding of the $11.76 price against an undisclosed share count, so soft. A tender price is a secondary clearing price, not a primary round valuation.

events.roundName: December 2024 private placement and former-employee tender
events.note: TWO PRICES IN THE SAME MONTH, and the modelling picks one. (a) The company sold 1,929,731 treasury shares to two accredited investors at $11.76 for $22.7M — cash in, recorded as amountRaisedUsd. (b) A tender opened in November 2024 for up to 2,000,000 shares held by FORMER employees closed in December at $10.00, repurchasing 1,355,459 shares for $13.6M — 15% below what current employees and outside buyers got in the same weeks. The $10.00 price was never reported in the press; it exists only in the S-1. The higher, better-sourced $11.76 is used, consistent with the conflict rule, and it is the same price as September's tender, so the $2B press rounding carries across unchanged rather than being re-derived. Both prices are real and the gap between them is the most interesting thing here.

curatorNotes: Nine preferred series and only two public post-money figures — Series F's $700M and Series G's disputed ~$500M. Everything else in the private history was reconstructed from the S-1 preferred-stock note (F-22), which prints authorized shares, issued shares and the issuance price for every series, so an amount raised exists for all nine even where no outlet ever wrote about the round. Series G-1's $25M has no press coverage anywhere on the internet. Two of the derived amounts are confirmed to the dollar by independent Form D filings (Series E $34,999,969, Series F $64,172,931). Series A-C were issued while the company was kaChing, a mutual-fund marketplace, which is why press series letters run two behind the charter throughout. Not modelled as events: the $2.187M of SAFEs outstanding at a $5.00 discounted price; ~1.64M common warrants issued 2019-2023 at a $2.60 weighted-average exercise price plus a TriplePoint lender warrant; a Series G warrant over 251,750 shares; and Andy Rachleff's $20M related-party Bridge Loan of January 2022, amended August 2023 and repaid November 2024 — debt, not equity. On the public side the pipeline is degraded and it matters: SEC XBRL carries only three dei cover-page share counts for WLTH (2026-01-22, 2026-04-22, 2026-06-11) and the fallback tags dedupe to four rows each, all under build_data.py's eight-row minimum, so no quarterly market cap is computed at all and the public series is the IPO-day override plus companiesmarketcap's annual points. The regression at 2025-12-31 therefore checks the companiesmarketcap slug and parse rather than a share tag. Hand cross-check of that point: the 2025-12-31 close was $13.59 and the 10-Q cover count as of 2026-01-22 was 150,120,383 shares, giving $2.04B — 5.2% ABOVE companiesmarketcap's $1.94B, which back-solves to about 142.75M shares, close to the 142.5M diluted weighted average. companiesmarketcap's current figure does track the cover count ($9.63 x 149,361,216 = $1.44B vs its $1.43B), so the discrepancy is confined to the year-end row. stockanalysis.com's daily history for WLTH begins 2025-12-15 and omits the first two sessions entirely, and has no Q4 2025 quarterly row; its own change field on 2025-12-15 (-1.69% to $13.95) implies a prior close of $14.19, which is exactly the first-day close the debut coverage reports, so the gap is a data defect rather than a later start date.
unresolved: Series A's issue date. The S-1 cap table prices it but never dates it; 2008 is inferred from the January 2008 rename and the December 2008 angel round, and 2007 is possible.

Series G-1's lead and participants. Exhibit 4.2's investor schedule is one combined list for all series, so the $25M cannot be attributed; Dragoneer, Maven Ventures Growth Labs and Second Line Advisors appear there and in no earlier round, but that is a guess and is not recorded as fact.
Whether Series G-1 priced before or after Series G. Both were closed by 2017-12-27 and G-1 was struck 25% higher, but nothing dates them relative to each other.
Post-money valuations for Series A, B, C, D, E and G-1 — six of nine rounds. None was ever published and none can be derived, because the fully diluted share count at each closing is not disclosed.

Quarterly market cap for WLTH. SEC XBRL has too few share-count rows to clear build_data.py's eight-row threshold, so nothing between 2025-12-12 and the annual points is computed; this resolves itself as more 10-Qs are filed.
companiesmarketcap's 2025 year-end figure is 5.2% below the SEC-cover-based calculation and its share basis for that row is unexplained.
